builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Double counting in LLM evidence fusion: exact posteriors separate rule compliance from posterior gain
summary: The technique replaces blanket 'count each source once' prompting heuristics in retrieval, multi-agent consensus, and agent memory with an exact-posterior benchmark and a paired-gain protocol that prices the instruction per receiver as a Brier difference on labelled deployment items. It costs only the construction of a small labelled evaluation set and paired raw-versus-instructed model calls; no training, extra inference at deployment, or infrastructure change is required. It can fail if the reader adopts the instruction universally, since the paper shows it degrades posterior accuracy in models that already comply with the rule, and its deployment estimate can mislead if labelled items do not match the true source-dependence structure.
rationale: The paper supplies a measurement protocol rather than a deployable optimization, and its core finding is that the same instruction helps some models and harms others, so the reader should run the cheap Brier-difference test on their own labelled items before adopting any evidence-fusion instruction.

claims.statement: The technique replaces blanket 'count each source once' prompting heuristics in retrieval, multi-agent consensus, and agent memory with an exact-posterior benchmark and a paired-gain protocol that prices the instruction per receiver as a Brier difference on labelled deployment items. It costs only the construction of a small labelled evaluation set and paired raw-versus-instructed model calls; no training, extra inference at deployment, or infrastructure change is required. It can fail if the reader adopts the instruction universally, since the paper shows it degrades posterior accuracy in models that already comply with the rule, and its deployment estimate can mislead if labelled items do not match the true source-dependence structure.

Instructing models to count each source once yields receiver-dependent Brier-score gains: gpt-6-luna gained 0.0140 (95% CI 0.0064-0.0219) at zero dependence, while for well-calibrated models the instruction increased posterior mismatch by 0.044; the prespecified delta=1 minus delta=0 contrast was 0.0342 (0.0303-0.0382).
